newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks end mostly lower on profit taking.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks end mostly lower on profit taking.

text.p: Asian stock markets, catching a breath after climbing to record highs, ended mostly lower on Wednesday as investors sold shares to consolidate gains.

Tokyo stocks ended slightly lower after profit taking eroded early additions to the previous day's gains, brokers said. But they said the losses were cushioned by small-lot buying by investors and some public funds.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 finished 32.74 points, or 0.15 percent lower at 21,397.19.
"It's natural that profit-taking emerged after the sudden rise on Tuesday of more than 400 points," a broker at a medium-sized brokerage said.
On Tuesday the Nikkei was boosted and Hong Kong and Australian bourses closed at record highs on momentum from Wall Street's advance past the key psychological 6000 level.

Wednesday's trading in Japan was mostly futures-linked rather than outright cash trade, brokers said. Although the market lacked motivation to propel it upwards, there were no waves of selling either.

"In the second half of the year, nearly two trillion yen worth of fresh funds is expected to enter the market via public funds so participants are reluctant to sell rapidly," Seiki Orimi, an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities said.
Brokers said foreign investors were about even as far as positions were concerned, opting to wait and see ahead of Japan's general election on October 20.
Hong Kong stocks ended sharply lower, after a morning surge to a new intra-day record high prompted investors to take profits during the afternoon, traders said.
The Hang Seng index closed 94.52 points lower at 12,396.18, well off the intra-day record of 12,602.34 hit earlier.
"I'm sure that what we have seen here is just a profit-taking session," said Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities.
Some brokers said rumours that First Pacific Co Ltd would place shares at a discount to its current market price sparked the profit-taking. First Pacific denied the rumours.

"The market obviously has risen very strongly over the last few days and needed to have a consolidation. The trigger of the consolidation was the rumour in the market of a possible placement of First Pacific. People used that as an excuse to top slice," said Remington.
Turnover soared to HK$9.142 billion, significantly higher than Tuesday's HK$8.41 billion.

In other trading, Australian shares ended slightly below their the previous day's record closing high. A mid-morning rally in resources issues helped the market. The benchmark All Ordinaries index finished 1.2 points lower at 2,365.

South Korean shares ended slightly higher after fluctuating for most of the day, trapped in a tug of war between profit-takers and bargain hunters. The index rose 6.58 points to a provisional close of 835.19, after ranging between 823.68 and 835.26. Advancing shares beat decliners 518 to 394.
Battered Thai stocks rebounded and were trading higher after falling for the past five consecutive trading days. Local investors bought actively bought finance issues, brokers said.
At 1130 GMT, the dollar traded at 112.15/2.20 yen and 1.5400/10 marks.
SIMEX Brent oil futures were backing off fresh five-year highs as some players took profits into the rally.
November was last traded at $25.07 per barrel, off the intraday high of $25.15, but still 34 cents above the London close on Tuesday of $24.73.
Hong Kong's gold market hardly moved, dealers said. Bullion opened at US$381.00/50 and closed at US$380.80/381.30.
